description: We are developing a web tool for the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. Our project helps users explore real NASA infrared images, compare observation dates and wavelengths, and investigate apparent changes in the sky. We are interested in astronomy, software development and making scientific data accessible.
summary: Our web prototype makes real NASA SPHEREx infrared observations easier to explore. Users select a sky field, browse images across observation dates, explore infrared wavelengths separately and compare observations. Actual exposure times, wavelength information and data gaps remain visible. The tool helps users investigate apparent changes while distinguishing visual differences from confirmed astronomical discoveries.
details:
We developed a web prototype for the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge that helps users explore how a selected patch of sky appears across observation dates and infrared wavelengths.

Users begin with a prepared example or select their own field using Right Ascension and declination. The application searches for actual SPHEREx observations and prepares images for inspection. A time control moves through available observation dates, while a separate wavelength control selects observations within a chosen date. Each image displays its actual observation time and wavelength. Users can pin a reference image, compare observations and export analysis parameters as JSON.

Separating time from wavelength is central to our approach. An image can look different because an object moved or changed brightness, but also because the observations cover different wavelengths, have missing pixels or contain instrumental effects. Our interface keeps these distinctions visible rather than presenting every difference as a discovery.

The application uses a React and TypeScript frontend with a Python and FastAPI backend. Scientific data handling uses tools including NumPy, Astropy, Astroquery and Reproject. The primary inputs are real SPHEREx FITS products retrieved from NASA/IPAC IRSA. SQLite and a file cache retain prepared analyses. Aladin Lite provides sky context.

Our documented checks cover all five fields requested by the challenge: Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae and R Draconis. These checks examined data availability and the suitability of selected observations for comparison. Coverage, quality flags and background limitations affected the results. We do not claim confirmed motion or variability for these five targets.

A separate example illustrates the apparent movement of the known comet 3I/ATLAS using real SPHEREx images. This demonstration is distinct from the five required target tests and does not represent a new discovery.

The submitted project is a locally runnable prototype. New archive searches require an internet connection, and previously prepared analyses depend on their stored data. Similar wavelength labels do not guarantee identical spectral responses, and visual comparisons alone do not establish scientific significance. Further calibration, validation and usability testing are needed.

Our goal is to make the first steps of exploring SPHEREx observations accessible without requiring users to write their own FITS-processing code.
